claims.text: MLIPs trained on strategically selected ab initio molecular-dynamics data near melting can reproduce the fusion free-energy landscapes of both solid and liquid phases with high fidelity.
The proposed MLIP workflow can reduce computational cost by up to an order of magnitude relative to TOR-TILD and explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Descriptors can be constructed that capture anharmonicity relevant to fusion thermodynamics.
MLIP descriptors can explicitly capture electron–vibration coupling.
High-entropy alloys are multicomponent metallic systems.
The approach is applicable to elemental metals and binary alloys and is extendable to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Anharmonic and electron–vibration effects are prominent near the melting point in the target materials.
A reduced training dataset can be obtained from focused ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations in the critical temperature region.
Descriptors encoding local vibrational behavior and electron–phonon coupling mediate accurate interpolation of solid and liquid free-energy surfaces.
Strategic sampling of only critical regions with ab initio molecular dynamics is sufficient for an MLIP to interpolate thermodynamic properties across the fusion transition.
The MLIP can faithfully retain the entropic contributions that would otherwise require expensive explicit sampling.
Focused MLIP training bypasses the need for full-scale molecular dynamics over extensive phase space.
The proposed method will predict phase free energies within a few meV per atom of full ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The proposed method will determine latent heat within approximately 5% of full ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
For complex multicomponent systems, the proposed method will be five to ten times faster than TOR-TILD.
The method should work near and slightly above the melting point, conditional on successful validation in simpler systems.
The accuracy of the method depends strongly on how representative the training data are.
Vibrational density of states can serve as a proxy for whether the model captures relevant entropic contributions.
